authoredSolutions.43: In \((x^2+\tfrac1{bx})^{11}\) the \(x^7\) term needs \(22-3r=7\Rightarrow r=5\), coefficient \(\binom{11}{5}b^{-5}\). In \((x-\tfrac1{bx^2})^{11}\) the \(x^{-7}\) term needs \(11-3r=-7\Rightarrow r=6\), coefficient \(\binom{11}{6}b^{-6}\). Since \(\binom{11}{5}=\binom{11}{6}\), \(b^{-5}=b^{-6}\Rightarrow b=1\).
authoredSolutions.44: Because \(g(x)=x\cos x\) is odd, \(\frac1{1+e^{g}}+\frac1{1+e^{-g}}=1\), so \(I=\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{dx}{\sin^4x+\cos^4x}\). Substituting \(t=\tan x\), \(\int_0^1\frac{1+t^2}{1+t^4}\,dt=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt2}\).
authoredSolutions.46: The left limit \((1+|\sin x|)^{3a/|\sin x|}\to e^{3a}\); the right limit's exponent \(\frac{\cot4x}{\cot2x}\to\tfrac12\), giving \(e^{1/2}\). Continuity forces \(e^{3a}=b=e^{1/2}\Rightarrow a=\tfrac16,\ b^2=e\), so \(6a+b^2=1+e\).
authoredSolutions.47: Squaring \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta=\tfrac12\) gives \(\sin2\theta=-\tfrac34\). Then \(\cos4\theta=1-2\sin^22\theta=-\tfrac18\) and \(\sin6\theta=3\sin2\theta-4\sin^32\theta=-\tfrac9{16}\). The bracket sums to \(-\tfrac{23}{16}\), and \(16\) times it is \(-23\).
authoredSolutions.48: \(2^n-2\equiv0\pmod3\Rightarrow(-1)^n\equiv-1\Rightarrow n\) is odd. Of the \(90\) two-digit numbers, \(45\) are odd, so the probability is \(\frac{45}{90}=\frac12\).

authoredSolutions.51: The mean gives \(\sum x=72\), and the known terms sum to \(60\), so \(a+b=12\). Variance \(\tfrac{37}{4}\Rightarrow\sum x^2=722\); the known squares sum to \(642\), so \(a^2+b^2=80\). Then \(2ab=144-80=64\) and \((a-b)^2=80-64=16\).
authoredSolutions.53: The AP condition is \((2^x-5)^2=2(2^x-\tfrac72)\). With \(t=2^x\): \(t^2-12t+32=0\Rightarrow t=8\) or \(4\); requiring \(t>5\) gives \(t=8\), so \(x=3\).
authoredSolutions.54: Using \(R_1\to R_1-R_3\) and \(R_2\to R_2-R_3\) and expanding, \(f(x)=4+2\cos2x\), which is maximised when \(\cos2x=1\): \(f_{\max}=6\).
authoredSolutions.55: \(f(x)=\min\{\{x\},\,1-\{x\}\}\) is a continuous triangular wave, so \(p=0\). On \([0,3]\) it has corner points at \(x=0.5,1,1.5,2,2.5\), giving \(q=5\); hence \(p+q=5\).
authoredSolutions.56: For \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\-1&4\end{bmatrix}\), \(\operatorname{tr}=5,\ \det=6\). By Cayley-Hamilton \(A^2-5A+6I=0\Rightarrow A^{-1}=\tfrac56 I-\tfrac16A\), so \(\alpha=\tfrac56,\ \beta=-\tfrac16\) and \(5(\alpha-\beta)=5\).
authoredSolutions.61: Since \(\sin(x+y)+\sin(x-y)=2\sin x\cos y\), the equation gives \(\sec x\,y'=2\sin x\cos y\Rightarrow y'=2\sin x\cos x\cos y\). At \(x=\tfrac\pi2\), \(\cos x=0\Rightarrow y'=0\), so \(5\,y'(\tfrac\pi2)=0\).
